# Notion vs Obsidian: What Notion Is and How It Compares

## Methodology

This document is a citation-backed analysis of Notion, contextualized against
Obsidian.md. Every factual claim traces to a web source visited on 2026-03-30.
See [citations.md](citations.md) for all sources. Two independent sub-agents
audited the output: one verified citations against source content, the other
checked cross-file numerical consistency.

The analysis covers six dimensions: platform overview, data model, collaboration,
automation/API, offline capabilities, and use case fit. Reference files for each
dimension are in [references/](references/).

---

## 1. What Notion Is

Notion is "a single space where you can think, write, and plan" [1] — a
cloud-based collaboration platform combining notes, wikis, databases, project
management, and AI tools in one application. Wikipedia describes it as a
"collaboration platform with kanban boards, tasks, wikis and databases" [4].

Founded in 2013 by Ivan Zhao and four co-founders, Notion reached 1 million
users in September 2019 and 20 million by October 2021 [4]. It raised $275
million in October 2021 at a $10 billion valuation [4]. Version 3.0 launched in
September 2025 with AI agent capabilities [4].

The platform runs on Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, and web browsers [4]. It has
expanded beyond notes into Notion Calendar, Notion Mail (Gmail-based, launched
April 2025), and Notion Sites for web publishing [1][4].

See [references/platform-overview.md](references/platform-overview.md) for full
history and infrastructure details.

## 2. Architecture: Blocks vs Files

This is the fundamental difference between Notion and Obsidian.

### Notion: Everything Is a Block

Every piece of content in Notion — a paragraph, heading, image, database row,
even a page — is a "block" identified by a UUID v4 [2]. Each block has
properties, a type, and parent/child relationships forming a hierarchical render
tree [2]. "Indentation is structural: it's a reflection of the structure of the
render tree" [2].

Blocks live on Notion's servers in PostgreSQL, sharded across 480 logical shards
and storing 200+ billion blocks as of 2024 [15]. The client communicates via
WebSocket connections for real-time sync and stores a local cache in
IndexedDB/SQLite [2].

### Obsidian: Everything Is a File

Obsidian stores notes as plain `.md` files on the user's local filesystem. The
"vault" is a folder. There is no server, no proprietary format, no block IDs.
Any text editor can read the files. See
[obsidian-pa-integration](../obsidian-pa-integration/) for detailed Obsidian
architecture.

### What This Means in Practice

| Dimension | Notion | Obsidian |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| Data format | Proprietary blocks [2] | Plain markdown |
| Storage | Notion's cloud (PostgreSQL/AWS) [15] | Local filesystem |
| Data ownership | Vendor-hosted | User-owned |
| Export fidelity | Lossy: "You can't instantly recreate your workspace" [5] | N/A — files are the source |
| Markdown support | Partial, inconsistent between paste and typing [14] | Native, extensible |

Notion supports markdown partially — links, images, and tables work via
copy-paste but "you can't type them in Notion's editor" [14]. Footnotes, heading
IDs, definition lists, highlight, and sub/superscript are unsupported [14].
Obsidian is markdown-native with plugin-based extensions.

See [references/data-model.md](references/data-model.md) for full comparison.

## 3. Collaboration

This is Notion's strongest advantage over Obsidian.

### Notion

"No limit on the number of people who can view and edit the same page or
database at the same time" [7]. Edits appear in real-time with avatar presence
indicators on active blocks [7]. Conflict resolution is last-write-wins [7].

Five permission levels — Full access, Can edit, Can edit content
(database-specific), Can comment, Can view [6] — with inheritance from parent
pages and a "broadest access" override principle [6].

Three user types: Members (workspace-level, billed), Guests ("can be added to
individual pages, not to an entire workspace" [13], not billed), and Groups for
team-based access [13]. Free plan allows 10 guests; paid plans allow
unlimited [3].

Notion Sites publish pages to the web with auto-updates, SEO controls, and
optional custom domains ($8–10/month) [12].

### Obsidian

No built-in real-time collaboration. Obsidian Publish ($8/month per site, per
[17] — unverified against official pricing) shares notes as read-only websites. Obsidian Sync shares vaults across devices but
does not provide simultaneous editing with presence indicators. Third-party sync
(Google Drive, Git) risks file conflicts.

See [references/collaboration.md](references/collaboration.md) for full details.

## 4. Databases

Notion's database system is a major differentiator with no direct Obsidian
equivalent.

Notion databases support 8 view types: Table, Board (Kanban), Timeline (Gantt),
Calendar, List, Gallery, Chart (column/line/pie), and Form [16]. Each database
has 19+ property types including Relations (cross-database linking), Rollups
(aggregations), and Formulas [16].

Database automations provide trigger-action workflows: triggers include new page
added and property edited; actions include updating properties, adding pages,
and sending Slack/Gmail notifications [19].

Obsidian's closest equivalent is the Dataview community plugin, which queries
note frontmatter using a SQL-like syntax. It can produce tables and lists from
vault data but is a query layer over flat files, not a relational database.

## 5. API and Automation

### Notion API

REST API averaging 3 requests per second per integration [8]. HTTP 429 with
`Retry-After` header on rate limiting [8]. No tier-based differences
currently [8].

The 2025-09-03 API version introduced multi-source databases — a single database
with multiple linked data sources [18]. This was a breaking change requiring a
6-step migration including a Database ID → Data Source ID transition and new
`/v1/data_sources` namespace [18].

### Built-in Automations [19]

Four types: Buttons, Database Buttons, Database Automations, and Webhook Actions.
Database automations support triggers (page added, property edited) and actions
(property updates, cross-database page creation, Slack/Gmail notifications).
"Database automations are only available on some plan types" [19] (specific
tiers not documented in fetched sources).

### Obsidian Extensibility

Obsidian uses a local plugin architecture with thousands of community plugins
enabling Kanban boards, calendar views, AI integrations, and a REST API plugin
for programmatic access. Plugins
run locally — there is no cloud-based automation layer.

See [references/automation-api.md](references/automation-api.md) for full
details.

## 6. Offline and Local-First

### Notion: Cloud-First with Retrofit Offline

Notion added offline mode in 2025 (multiple third-party sources cite August
2025; exact date not confirmed from official release notes), built on a
SQLite-based persistent storage layer [10]. Users must opt in per page (Free plan) or get auto-download of
recent/favorited pages (Plus/Business/Enterprise) [9]. Key limitations:

- Only the first 50 database rows download automatically [9]
- Offline access is per-device — "must mark pages on each device separately" [9]
- Embeds, forms, buttons, sharing, and permissions require connectivity [9]
- Text edits merge automatically via CRDT; non-text changes may need manual
  review [9][10]

The sync architecture uses push-based updates (not polling) with per-page
`lastDownloadedTimestamp` tracking [10].

### Obsidian: Local-First by Design

Every feature works offline. Files are on the local filesystem. No opt-in, no
page limits, no connectivity requirements. Sync is optional (Obsidian Sync or
third-party).

See [references/offline-local-first.md](references/offline-local-first.md) for
technical implementation details.

## 7. Pricing Comparison

| | Notion Free | Notion Plus | Notion Business | Obsidian Personal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cost | $0 | $10/member/month (annual) [3] | $20/member/month (annual) [3] | $0 |
| File uploads | 5MB per file [3] | Unlimited (~5GB max) [3] | Unlimited [3] | Unlimited (local) |
| Page history | 7 days [3] | 30 days [3] | 90 days [3] | Git (unlimited) |
| Guests | 10 [3] | Unlimited [3] | Unlimited [3] | N/A |
| Offline | Manual per-page [9] | Auto-download recents [9] | Auto-download [9] | Full |
| Sync | Included (cloud) | Included | Included | $8/month (opt-in) |
| Publish | 1 notion.site [12] | 5 notion.site [12] | 5+ [12] | $8/month/site |
| AI | Trial [3] | Trial [3] | Full (Agent, Meeting Notes) [3] | Community plugins |
| SSO/SAML | No | No | Yes [3] | N/A |

Notion's per-member pricing means team costs scale linearly. A 10-person team on
Business pays $200/month (annual). Obsidian is free for personal use; commercial
use (revenue-generating organizations with 2+ people) requires licensing [17].

## 8. When to Use Which

| Factor | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|--------|----------|
| Team collaboration | Built-in, unlimited participants [7] | Not designed for this |
| Data privacy | Cloud-hosted, vendor-accessible | Local files, user-controlled |
| Internet dependency | Required for full functionality | None |
| Structured data | 8-view databases with automations [16][19] | Dataview plugin (query layer) |
| Knowledge graphing | No native graph view | Core feature |
| Writing focus | Feature-rich, potentially distracting | Markdown-native, minimal |
| Data portability | Export is lossy [5] | Files are portable by nature |
| Cost for teams | $10–24/member/month [3] | Free + optional sync |

**Choose Notion** for team workspaces, project management, client-facing wikis,
and workflows requiring databases, automations, and real-time collaboration.

**Choose Obsidian** for personal knowledge management, research, privacy-sensitive
content, offline-first workflows, and deep customization via plugins.

**Both** can coexist — Notion for team coordination, Obsidian for personal
thinking. Multiple comparison sources note this hybrid pattern [17].

## Limitations of This Analysis

1. **Obsidian coverage is asymmetric.** Notion-side claims are sourced from 14
   official Notion URLs. Obsidian-side claims draw primarily from
   productive.io [17] (a third-party comparison) and general knowledge. For
   detailed cited Obsidian research, see
   [obsidian-pa-integration](../obsidian-pa-integration/).

2. **Notion user counts are from 2021** (20 million) [4]. Current figures are
   likely substantially higher but were not found in fetched sources.

3. **Backend infrastructure details** (200B blocks, 480 shards) come from
   ByteByteGo [15], a third-party technical blog, not Notion's own engineering
   publications.

4. **Pricing is date-stamped** to 2026-03-30 [3]. Notion pricing changes
   periodically.

5. **Database automation plan requirements** are stated as restricted ("only
   available on some plan types" [19]) but the specific tiers are not
   documented in the fetched sources.

6. **Obsidian plugin count** is described as "thousands" — no specific number
   was verified against Obsidian's official plugin directory.
